title: Instant Pot Vietnamese-Style Bò Kho with Carrots & Noodles
dek: Aromatic beef and honeycomb tripe become tender in a star-anise tomato broth, with carrots, daikon and noodles added in stages so every component keeps its shape.
image_alt: Vietnamese-style bò kho with beef chunks, honeycomb tripe, large carrot pieces, daikon and noodles in a red aromatic broth
ingredients: 1 3/4 lb boneless beef chuck, trimmed and cut into 1 1/2-inch pieces
8 oz cleaned honeycomb beef tripe, cut into 1-inch strips
1 lemongrass stalk, tender inner part bruised and cut in half
1 lb carrots, peeled and cut into 2-inch pieces
8 oz daikon radish, peeled and cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
1/2 cup cilantro and Thai basil leaves
Sliced fresh chile or chile oil, optional for serving

instructions.name: Season the beef and tripe
instructions.text: Pat the beef and cleaned tripe dry. Season with 1 teaspoon salt. Keep the beef pieces uniform so they tenderize at the same rate.

instructions.name: Build the aromatic base
instructions.text: Select Sauté on Normal on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Heat the oil, brown the beef in two batches for about 3 minutes per batch and transfer it to a plate. Add onion and cook 3 minutes. Stir in garlic, ginger, tomato paste, paprika and five-spice for 45 seconds; cancel Sauté before the paste scorches.

instructions.name: Deglaze with thin broth
instructions.text: Pour in the beef broth and scrape the base until completely smooth. Stir in fish sauce, brown sugar and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Return the beef and its juices, then add tripe, star anise and lemongrass. Keep the pot below the model's maximum-fill line.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook the meat
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 24 minutes; allow about 15 minutes to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses. Pause if broth sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Add the vegetables
instructions.text: Remove the lid, stir in carrots and daikon, and make sure the valve area is clear. Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 3 minutes; allow 6 to 8 minutes to repressurize. Use a controlled quick release, pausing if liquid sputters.

instructions.name: Verify doneness and adjust
instructions.text: Remove star anise and lemongrass. Beef should be fork-tender and at least 145°F; the tripe should reach 160°F. If either is not tender or at temperature, simmer on Sauté Low until ready. Taste and add fish sauce or broth as needed.

instructions.name: Cook noodles and serve
instructions.text: While the vegetables cook, prepare noodles according to the package and drain. Divide noodles among bowls, ladle over the red broth with beef, tripe, carrots and daikon, and finish with sprouts, herbs and lime. Keep the pot mild and offer chile at the table.

why_it_works: Browning adds savory depth, while a thorough broth deglaze removes concentrated tomato paste from the base before pressure builds.
Cooking the meat first and adding large root-vegetable pieces for a short second cycle keeps the carrots and daikon recognizable instead of mushy.
Noodles cook separately, so their starch cannot thicken the pressure-cooker liquid or trigger a burn warning.
swaps: For a tripe-free version, use 2 1/4 lb beef chuck and keep the same pressure timing.
Rice noodles can replace wheat noodles for a gluten-free bowl; verify that the fish sauce and broth are gluten-free.
Turnips can replace daikon, but cut them into 2-inch pieces because they soften faster.
storage: Cool stew and noodles separately in shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate stew for up to 4 days and noodles for up to 3 days. Reheat stew to 165°F, adding broth if needed; warm noodles separately. Freeze the stew without noodles, sprouts or herbs for up to 3 months.
notes: Total time includes two pressurizing stages, both programmed cycles, a 10-minute natural release, controlled venting and noodle preparation.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your model manual for minimum liquid, maximum fill and venting, and never force the lid.
Use cleaned, food-ready honeycomb tripe from a reliable butcher. Wash hands, utensils and surfaces after handling raw beef or tripe.
Keep the broth mild for the shared pot. Fresh chile and chile oil belong at the table, away from young children.
Do not add the noodles to the cooker before pressure; they would absorb the measured thin liquid and may stick to the base.

faqs.q: Can I skip the second pressure cycle?
faqs.a: Yes. After the 24-minute meat cycle, simmer the carrots and daikon uncovered on Sauté Low for 12 to 18 minutes. This takes slightly longer but makes it easy to monitor texture.

faqs.q: Is bò kho supposed to be a soup or a stew?
faqs.a: It can be served either way. This version has enough aromatic broth for noodles, like the photographed bowl; reduce it on Sauté for a thicker stew to serve with baguette.

faqs.q: Why is my beef still chewy?
faqs.a: Chuck varies in connective tissue and piece size. Simmer it gently after pressure or cook for another 5-minute pressure cycle, then recheck tenderness and temperature.

title: Instant Pot Egyptian-Style Ful Medames Breakfast Platter
dek: Creamy whole fava beans pressure-cook from an overnight soak, then become a lemon-cumin breakfast platter with warm pita, pickles, tomato and peppery greens.
image_alt: Egyptian-style ful medames breakfast platter with a bowl of fava beans, pita breads, pickled vegetables, tomato salad and fresh rocket leaves
ingredients: 1 lb dried small brown fava beans, sorted and rinsed
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for serving
1 cup mixed pickled turnips, carrots or cucumbers
Aleppo pepper or hot sauce, optional for serving

instructions.name: Soak the fava beans
instructions.text: Cover the beans with at least 3 inches of cool water and soak 8 to 12 hours. Drain and rinse. Discard any stones or damaged beans.

instructions.name: Load the cooker safely
instructions.text: Put the drained beans in a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Add 4 1/2 cups fresh water, onion, 2 whole garlic cloves, bay leaf and 1/2 teaspoon cumin. Do not add salt or oil yet. The cooker must remain below the half-full line because beans expand and foam.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 35 minutes; allow about 15 minutes to come to pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 20 minutes, then vent any remainder in short controlled pulses. Pause if foam or liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Check tenderness
instructions.text: Remove the bay leaf and onion. Crush several beans against the side of the pot; they should mash without a chalky center. If firm, add 1/2 cup hot water if the pot looks dry and cook for 5 more minutes with a full natural release.

instructions.name: Season and mash
instructions.text: Finely grate the remaining 2 garlic cloves into the beans. Stir in 1 teaspoon cumin, 1 teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons olive oil and the lemon juice. Mash about one-third of the beans, leaving the rest whole. Simmer on Sauté Low for 3 to 5 minutes if the mixture is loose, then cancel.

instructions.name: Build the breakfast platter
instructions.text: Combine tomatoes and parsley with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Spoon ful into a shallow bowl, drizzle with the remaining olive oil and arrange it on a platter with warm pita, pickles, tomato salad and rocket leaves to match the photograph. Offer Aleppo pepper or hot sauce separately.

why_it_works: An overnight soak helps small favas hydrate evenly; cooking them in ample plain water lets their skins soften before salt and acid are added.
A full natural release controls foaming and gives the bean centers time to finish gently.
Partial mashing thickens the cooking liquid naturally, while lemon, garlic and cumin added after pressure stay bright and aromatic.
swaps: If small brown favas are unavailable, use dried broad beans labeled for ful; very large favas may need 5 to 10 additional pressure-cook minutes.
For a gluten-free platter, replace pita with gluten-free flatbread or roasted potatoes.
Chopped romaine or watercress can replace rocket leaves, and any crisp vinegar pickle works beside the beans.
storage: Cool the beans in shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat on the stove or microwave until steaming hot, thinning with water; store pita, pickles and fresh vegetables separately.
notes: Total time excludes the unattended overnight soak but includes about 15 minutes to pressurize, the 35-minute cycle, a 20-minute natural release and finishing time.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your model manual for minimum liquid, bean fill limits and venting, and never force the lid.
Beans and their liquid must stay below the half-full line. Do not double this recipe in a 6-quart cooker.
Bean age affects timing. Judge doneness by a creamy center, not only by the programmed time.
The shared bowl is warmly seasoned but not hot; add Aleppo pepper or hot sauce at the table.

faqs.q: Can I make ful without soaking the beans?
faqs.a: A no-soak batch is possible but less predictable: pressure-cook for 55 minutes and allow a complete natural release, then check several beans. Older beans may still need another cycle.

faqs.q: Why should I wait to add lemon and salt?
faqs.a: Acid can slow softening and early salt makes it harder to judge seasoning as the liquid reduces. Adding both after the beans are creamy gives more reliable texture and brighter flavor.
No. Serve the same platter for lunch or a light supper, or pack the beans and vegetables separately for meal prep.

title: Japanese Oyakodon with Chicken, Egg & Steamed Rice
dek: Tender chicken and onion simmer in a savory-sweet dashi sauce, then softly set eggs blanket hot rice for a complete 30-minute bowl.
image_alt: Japanese oyakodon bowl with pieces of chicken, softly set golden egg, translucent onion and mitsuba over steamed rice
ingredients: 1 3/4 cups water, or the amount specified for the rice
1 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into 1-inch pieces
6 large eggs, preferably pasteurized if a softer set is desired
1/2 cup loosely packed mitsuba leaves and stems, or sliced scallions

instructions.name: Cook the rice
instructions.text: Combine rinsed rice and water in a rice cooker or saucepan and cook according to the package. Keep covered and warm while the topping cooks.

instructions.name: Season the chicken
instructions.text: Pat chicken dry, season with salt and separate the pieces so they cook evenly.

instructions.name: Simmer the onion
instructions.text: In a 10-inch skillet, combine dashi, soy sauce, mirin and sugar. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, add onion and cook for 4 minutes until slightly softened.

instructions.name: Cook the chicken safely
instructions.text: Add chicken in one layer, cover and simmer gently for 6 to 8 minutes, turning once. Check several of the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer; each must reach 165°F.

instructions.name: Add the eggs in two pours
instructions.text: Beat the eggs just enough to break the whites and yolks while leaving visible streaks. Pour two-thirds evenly around the skillet, cover and cook 60 to 90 seconds. Add the remaining egg and mitsuba, cover and cook 45 to 90 seconds more, until the egg dish reaches 160°F. Use pasteurized eggs and local guidance if intentionally serving softer.

instructions.name: Build the bowls
instructions.text: Divide hot rice among four bowls. Slide the chicken, softly set egg, onion and sauce over the rice, keeping the large golden curds and green garnish visible like the photograph. Serve immediately.

why_it_works: Chicken thighs stay juicy through the covered simmer, while the shallow skillet gives the pieces room to cook evenly.
Two egg additions create fully set curds underneath and a softer-looking golden surface without losing the 160°F safety target.
Dashi, soy and mirin season both the chicken and rice, so the bowl tastes complete with a short ingredient list.
swaps: Use boneless chicken breast cut into 3/4-inch pieces and begin checking at 5 minutes to prevent drying.
For an alcohol-free version, replace mirin with 2 tablespoons water plus 1 tablespoon sugar and 1 teaspoon rice vinegar.
Long-grain rice works, though short-grain rice better catches the sauce and matches the photographed bowl.
storage: Cool the topping and rice in separate shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat each separately until the chicken, egg and rice reach 165°F; add a spoonful of water before reheating the topping.
notes: Have the rice cooking before starting the skillet so the meal truly lands in 30 minutes.
Do not crowd chicken into a smaller pan; overlapping pieces cook unevenly.
Eggs continue setting after the heat is off, so move the topping to the bowls as soon as it reaches 160°F.
Mitsuba gives the most traditional green aroma, but scallions are easier to find and visually similar.
Chicken must reach 165°F and the egg mixture 160°F; check temperature rather than relying on color alone.

faqs.q: Why does my egg turn rubbery?
faqs.a: The skillet is likely boiling too hard or sitting covered too long. Keep the sauce at a gentle simmer, use the two-pour method and serve as soon as the egg reaches 160°F.

faqs.q: Can I cook all four servings at once?
faqs.a: Yes in a 10- to 12-inch skillet. For smaller pans, make two half batches so the chicken stays in one layer.
Yes. Mix it according to the package and choose a reduced-sodium option if available because soy sauce also contributes salt.

title: Portuguese Bacalhau à Brás with Olives & Parsley
dek: Flaked salt cod, sweet onion and crisp matchstick potatoes fold into softly set eggs, then finish with black olives and parsley for a classic Lisbon-style supper.
image_alt: Portuguese bacalhau à Brás with shredded salt cod, golden matchstick potatoes and softly set egg topped with black olives and parsley
ingredients: 8 large eggs, preferably pasteurized if a softer set is desired

instructions.name: Desalt the cod
instructions.text: Place salt cod in a nonreactive bowl, cover with cold water and refrigerate for 24 to 36 hours, changing the water every 8 hours. Taste a tiny cooked flake; it should be pleasantly seasoned, not aggressively salty. Drain and pat dry.

instructions.name: Poach and flake the cod
instructions.text: Put cod in a saucepan, cover with fresh water and bring just to a simmer. Cook 6 to 8 minutes, until opaque and the thickest part reaches 145°F. Drain, cool slightly, remove any bones and flake into bite-size pieces.

instructions.name: Cut and rinse the potatoes
instructions.text: Cut potatoes into 1/8-inch matchsticks with a mandoline or knife. Rinse in several changes of cold water, drain and dry very thoroughly between clean towels.

instructions.name: Fry the potatoes
instructions.text: Heat neutral oil in a deep heavy pot to 350°F, keeping it no more than half full. Fry potatoes in four batches for 3 to 4 minutes until pale gold and crisp. Transfer to a rack or paper towels and let the oil return to 350°F between batches.

instructions.name: Soften the onions
instructions.text: Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-low. Add onions and cook 10 to 12 minutes until soft and lightly golden. Stir in garlic for 30 seconds, then fold in the flaked cod.

instructions.name: Fold in potatoes and eggs
instructions.text: Beat eggs with black pepper. Reserve one-quarter of the potatoes for garnish and fold the rest into the cod. Reduce heat to low, pour in eggs and stir gently for 2 to 4 minutes until creamy curds form and the egg mixture reaches 160°F. Use pasteurized eggs and local guidance if intentionally serving softer.

instructions.name: Garnish and serve
instructions.text: Spoon onto a warm platter, mound the reserved crisp potatoes over the top, and scatter with black olives and parsley to match the photograph. Serve immediately with lemon wedges.

why_it_works: Repeated cold-water changes remove excess salt without stripping the cod of all its seasoning.
Rinsing and thoroughly drying thin potato matchsticks promotes crispness and reduces dangerous splattering in hot oil.
Reserving some potatoes until the end preserves a crisp contrast while the rest soften slightly in the creamy egg and cod mixture.
swaps: For a faster weeknight version, use 10 oz plain potato sticks and reduce additional seasoning because the snack contributes salt.
Fresh cod can replace salt cod; poach it to 145°F and season the finished skillet gradually with kosher salt.
Green olives give a sharper flavor than black olives but still provide the briny garnish.
storage: Cool within 2 hours and refrigerate in a shallow container for up to 2 days. Reheat gently in a covered skillet or microwave until the cod and egg mixture reach 165°F. The potatoes soften in storage; refresh reserved potatoes separately in a 375°F oven.
notes: Total time excludes the 24- to 36-hour refrigerated desalting period.
Salt cod varies widely. Taste a cooked flake before assembling and avoid adding salt until the final adjustment.
Use a deep pot, keep oil below the halfway point and never add wet potatoes to hot oil.
A mandoline makes uniform matchsticks but requires the hand guard and a cut-resistant glove.
Cod must reach 145°F; the finished egg mixture should reach 160°F unless pasteurized eggs and local guidance support a softer set.

faqs.q: Can I bake the potatoes instead of frying?
faqs.a: Yes. Toss matchsticks with 2 tablespoons oil and bake in a single layer at 425°F for 20 to 28 minutes, turning once. They will be less delicate but still provide crisp contrast.

faqs.q: Why is my bacalhau à Brás watery?
faqs.a: The cod or potatoes were probably not drained well, or the onions held extra moisture. Dry each component carefully and let the onion-cod mixture cook uncovered before adding eggs.

faqs.q: Can I desalt the cod more quickly?
faqs.a: Smaller pieces desalinate faster, but rushing at room temperature is unsafe and uneven. Keep the cod refrigerated in cold water and change it regularly.

title: French Tarte Tatin with Caramelized Apples
dek: Deeply bronzed apples bake beneath crisp butter pastry, then flip into a glossy upside-down tart with clear caramel and unmolding cues.
image_alt: Whole French tarte Tatin with glossy deeply caramelized apple wedges arranged over a round pastry base
ingredients: 1 sheet (14 oz) all-butter puff pastry, thawed but cold
3 lb firm tart-sweet apples, such as Pink Lady and Granny Smith
6 tbsp unsalted butter, cut into pieces
Crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream, for serving

instructions.name: Prepare the pastry
instructions.text: Roll the cold puff pastry into a 12-inch round. Place on parchment, prick lightly with a fork and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes while preparing the apples.

instructions.name: Cut and season the apples
instructions.text: Peel, quarter and core the apples. Toss with lemon juice. Keep the quarters large; they shrink during the stovetop and oven cooking.

instructions.name: Make the caramel
instructions.text: Heat sugar in a 10-inch oven-safe skillet over medium heat without stirring, swirling only after the edges melt. Cook until evenly amber, 6 to 9 minutes. Remove from heat and carefully whisk in butter, salt, vanilla and cinnamon; the mixture will bubble vigorously.

instructions.name: Arrange and pre-cook
instructions.text: Pack apple quarters tightly in concentric circles, rounded sides down. Return the skillet to medium-low and cook 18 to 22 minutes, spooning caramel over the fruit, until the apples begin to soften and the liquid becomes syrupy.

instructions.name: Cover with pastry
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 400°F. Drape the chilled pastry over the apples, tuck the edge carefully inside the skillet and cut three small steam vents in the center.

instructions.name: Bake until deeply golden
instructions.text: Bake 28 to 35 minutes, until the pastry is deeply golden and crisp and caramel bubbles around the edge. If using a thermometer, the center of the pastry should be about 200°F. Cool in the skillet for 15 minutes—long enough for the caramel to thicken, but not set hard.

instructions.name: Invert safely
instructions.text: Run a thin knife around the edge. Wearing oven mitts, center a rimmed serving plate over the skillet and invert in one confident motion. Lift the skillet away from your body. Replace any stuck apples and spoon caramel over the glossy fruit to match the photograph.

why_it_works: Two firm apple varieties balance acidity and sweetness while holding their shape through both stovetop caramelizing and baking.
Pre-cooking drives off apple juice before pastry is added, preventing a watery caramel and soggy base.
A 15-minute rest lets bubbling caramel become syrupy enough to coat the apples without hardening them to the pan.
swaps: Use a 12-ounce round of homemade rough puff pastry if preferred; keep it cold before baking.
Firm pears can replace half the apples, but choose underripe fruit and expect a slightly softer arrangement.
For a dairy-free tart, use vegan puff pastry and a firm plant-based baking butter with similar fat content.
storage: Tarte Tatin is best the day it is baked. Cover and refrigerate leftovers for up to 3 days. Reheat slices on a sheet pan at 350°F for 8 to 12 minutes; avoid the microwave if you want the pastry crisp. Do not freeze the assembled tart because the apples release water as they thaw.
notes: Total time includes a 20-minute pastry chill and a 15-minute cooling window before inversion.
Caramel is extremely hot. Keep children away from the stove and oven during cooking and unmolding.
Use an oven-safe 10-inch skillet with no plastic or wood components; a cast-iron skillet produces steady caramelization.
If the caramel smells bitter or turns nearly black, discard it carefully after cooling and start again.
Choose a serving plate with a rim because warm caramel can run when the tart is inverted.

faqs.q: Why did my apples stick to the skillet?
faqs.a: The tart probably cooled too long. Warm the skillet over low heat for 30 to 60 seconds to loosen the caramel, then invert again with oven mitts.

faqs.q: Can I assemble the tart ahead?
faqs.a: You can cook and arrange the apples up to 4 hours ahead, cool and refrigerate them in the skillet, then add cold pastry and bake. Add 5 to 10 minutes because the skillet starts cold.

faqs.q: Why is my puff pastry soggy?
faqs.a: The apples released too much liquid or the pastry was warm. Reduce the apple juices to a thick syrup before covering, chill the pastry well and bake until deeply golden rather than merely pale.
